newsitem.title: USA: Documentary on death of Yugoslavia wins top TV honour.
newsitem.headline: Documentary on death of Yugoslavia wins top TV honour.

text.p: "The Death of Yugoslavia," a five-part series made for the BBC and the U.S. Discovery Channel by Britain's Brian Lapping Associates, won the Gold Baton, the highest honour of the Alfred I. duPont-Columbia University boradcasting awards on Thursday night.

The series, narrated by Cable News Network's Christiane Amanpour, details the dismemberment of Yugoslavia and, according to the citation it received, "carefully explains how Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic systematically and brutally increased the territory under his control."

The ABC programme "Nightline" was cited with a Silver Baton for three programs: a week-long examination of the verdict in the O.J. Simpson trial, a two-part piece on treating AIDS patients and a two-hour debate in Israel after the assassination of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin called, "Town Meeting: Thou Shall Not Kill."

The CBS programme "60 Minutes" received a Silver Baton for two segments, "Punishing Saddam," a report on the devastating impact of sanctions on ordinary Iraqis, and "Too Good to Be True," a report on the success of a private school in a poor neigborhood."

NBC's "Dateline" programme received a Silver Baton for "Class Photo," a project that took nine months to make in which members of a 1982 fourth-grade class at a Brooklyn ghetto school were tracked down. The report discovered that the women were successful, while many of the men in the class were in prison or had been involved in crime.

The PBS programme NOVA, the PBS network and WGBH in Boston were given a Silver Baton for their report on the fight in Zaire against the deadly plague Ebola. A NOVA crew was was the only film crew allowed in the "hot zone" of the epidemic near Kikwit and risked their lives to film "the heroic scientific war against the disease."

A three-hour Frontline programme on PBS called "Shtetl" was also given a Silver Baton. The programme recorded the journey of filmmaker Marian Marzynski to his native Poland to see what was left of the Jewish village he grew up in.
